label: Resonator spectroscopy vs flux
axes: A 2-D colour map per qubit (one panel, or a grid of panels with one qubit named per panel). Horizontal axis: the flux bias swept on that qubit's flux line, sometimes with a twin top axis restating the very same sweep in the alternative bias convention (it is one variable, not two). Vertical axis: the readout drive frequency swept at each bias point. Colour: the measured readout response amplitude, in which the resonator appears as a dark band winding across the map (verify the polarity from the panel itself — the response is whichever tone forms the continuous narrow band against uniform background texture). Overlays vary by plotter generation: newer figures draw small open circles for the per-column extracted dip position, a smooth periodic fit curve through them, a dashed vertical marker at the claimed upper-extremum bias and a second dashed vertical at the claimed lower-extremum bias, plus a coverage badge in the panel title; older figures draw only a marker point on the band plus the dashed verticals, with no fit curve.
correct_signature: One continuous dark band spans the full width of the map, unbroken from column to column, distinctly darker than the surrounding speckle along its whole length, and roughly constant in thickness.

The band's vertical position varies smoothly and periodically with the bias sweep: a single smooth arc when the swept range holds less than one modulation period, or repeating crests and troughs of equal height and even spacing when it holds more than one.

Where a fit curve is drawn it lies within the band's own thickness at essentially every column, not merely near the marked extremum; where per-column dip circles are drawn, the large majority sit on that curve and strays are isolated rather than forming their own competing track.

The dashed marker for the claimed extremum meets the band exactly where the band's own turning point is: the band rises on one side and falls on the other, and is symmetric about the marker over at least a couple of band thicknesses either way.

When both an upper and a lower extremum marker are drawn they sit at opposite turning points of the same modulation — one where the band is highest, one where it is lowest — separated by about half the visible modulation period.

When more than one crest is visible, successive crests sit at the same level as one another and successive troughs likewise, so the modulation reads as stationary across the sweep rather than tilted or growing.
Away from the band the map is featureless texture: no second band of comparable darkness crossing or shadowing the first, and no full-height stripe as dark as the band.

failure_appearance.wrong_peak: The band is present and traceable, but the dashed extremum marker does not meet it at a turning point: it lands where the band is still climbing or falling monotonically, so the band is visibly asymmetric about the marker, or it lands on one of several equally dark lobes with no single resolved turning point between them. A fit curve may still hug the band over much of the sweep while its own crest is displaced from the band's crest by more than the band's thickness.
failure_appearance.noisy: Speckle contrast approaches the band's own contrast: the band is only a shade darker than its surroundings, its edges are ragged, its apparent centre wanders by a good fraction of its thickness between neighbouring columns, and it thins into the background for stretches of consecutive columns. Per-column dip circles then scatter above and below the fit instead of lying on it. Panels of this quality do occur among accepted runs, so grain by itself is not disqualifying — what matters is whether one continuous band and a symmetric turning point can still be traced by eye.
failure_appearance.feature_present_fit_failed: A clear continuous dark band is there, but nothing in the overlay expresses an extremum on it: no fit curve and no marker point on the band, or the extremum markers pinned against the boundary of the swept range while the band is still rising or falling as it leaves the window — a real resonator response with no turning point bracketed inside the sweep for a periodic model to lock onto.

abstain_when: The band's total vertical excursion across the whole sweep is no larger than the band's own thickness, so the map is effectively a flat stripe and no turning point is resolvable by eye — such panels are legitimately accepted, so abstain rather than reject.
The figure is a grid of panels and the panel corresponding to the claim cannot be identified, or that panel is blank, missing its band, or rendered at a size where the band is a few pixels thick.
The overlay carries no fit curve and no extremum marker at all, so the picture contains nothing that expresses the numeric claim being checked.
The colour scale is saturated or compressed so that most of the map is one flat tone and the band's edges are indistinguishable from background, making the turning point unlocatable.

Several equivalent crests (or troughs) of the same modulation are in view and the overlay marks one of them: judge only whether the marked point is a genuine turning point, and abstain on which repeat was chosen unless the claim itself says.

The extremum markers sit at the boundary of the swept bias range with the band still rising or falling as it leaves the window - no turning point was bracketed, so report the bracketing problem rather than a verdict.
notes:
Evidence is thin and one-sided. Only one run of this family is stated to be node-accepted; no node-rejected run is archived, so nothing here is calibrated against a known-bad example. I opened six archived figures across several chips and plotter generations to widen the sample, but every one of them is an unlabeled or accepted run. Consequently `no_signal` and `drifted` are null: I never saw a panel with no band at all, and never saw successive crests landing at different levels, so I refuse to describe how either would look. The stationary-crest bullet in correct_signature is what a judge should check drift against instead. `wrong_peak` and `feature_present_fit_failed` are written from appearances I did see in unlabeled archived runs (a marker sitting on a broad multi-lobed dark region with no single turning point; a full multi-panel figure whose bands are real but carry no fit curve and whose offset markers sit at the sweep boundary) — treat them as descriptions of shape, not as verdicts the node itself issued.

Two plotter generations coexist within this family and both appear in accepted archives: an older one with only a marker point plus dashed verticals and no fit curve or coverage badge, and a newer one with per-column dip circles, a smooth periodic fit and a coverage percentage in the panel title. The judge must not treat the absence of a fit curve as evidence of failure by itself — see abstain_when.

Two traps specific to this family. First, the twin top axis is the same bias sweep restated in the other convention; reading it as an independent variable will produce nonsense. Second, the swept range legitimately covers anywhere from a fraction of one modulation period (a shallow arc, sometimes nearly flat) to several full periods (many crests); both extremes are accepted, so period count carries no information about correctness on its own. Near-flat bands are common and accepted — flatness must route to abstain, never to reject.

localizer is "none": this is a 2-D map and the trustworthy signature is the joint geometry of the band, the fit and the markers. The bias offset alone cannot be pointed at on a single axis without the band, so this family is signature-trust-only.
